LESSON 50 OF 106·Identity, Authentication and Access Control

Privilege Escalation and Admin Account Hygiene

How a routine account gains rights it was never granted, why standing admin access is the real problem, and the hygiene that keeps elevation rare.

Foundation13 min
Why this matters

Privilege escalation turns a limited foothold into control of the system. Most of it succeeds because of ordinary configuration mistakes rather than clever exploitation.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Escalation means moving from one level of access to a higher one, either by exploiting a flaw or by abusing a permissive setting.
  • Misconfigured service permissions, over-broad file permissions and unattended administrative sessions are the usual route.
  • Scheduled tasks and services are frequently configured to run with more privilege than the work requires.
  • Administrator accounts used for daily work turn any credential theft into full control immediately.
  • Separating a standard account from an administrative one makes this class of escalation much harder.

The background

  • Local privilege escalation was largely about predictable service paths and permissive file permissions.
  • Kernel and driver exploits were the high-profile route, and are still the route when configuration is sound.
  • Token and impersonation features gave applications ways to act as other users, which is powerful and frequently misconfigured.
  • Current guidance is dominated by removing the permissions that made escalation possible in the first place.

Real-world examples

  • A service that can read a file only administrators should read is a complete escalation path on its own.
  • An unquoted service path lets an attacker place an executable earlier in the search order and run it as the service.
  • A single administrative account for an entire team means one stolen laptop is a domain compromise.

What to look for

  • Check service and task permissions, since these are the most common local escalation path.
  • Check whether the administrative accounts used day to day are separate from standard user accounts.
  • Check file permissions on program directories and configuration files.
  • Check how many accounts are administrators, since more than a handful is a finding in itself.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Run day-to-day work as a standard user and elevate only for specific tasks.
  • Give services the minimum privilege they need, and check their file and directory permissions.
  • Use absolute or quoted paths in service definitions so an attacker cannot substitute a binary.
  • Give each administrator a separate named account, and use just-in-time elevation where available.
  • Monitor for new members of privileged groups, which is the event that precedes most escalation chains.
